h: The laird, the archaeologist and the house you can step inside
p: When the great storm of 1850 ripped the grass off the dunes, it was the local laird, William Watt of Skaill, who began digging into what had been revealed. His family home, Skaill House, still stands next to the site, a fine seventeenth-century mansion that adds a completely different chapter to a visit. It's a fun contrast: you go from Stone Age dressers to the laird's dining room in a few minutes' walk.

The proper scientific dig came later, in the 1920s, led by the archaeologist V. Gordon Childe, who did much to explain how the village worked. People are thought to have lived here for several centuries, from roughly 3200 BC onwards, before the village was abandoned.

Don't miss the replica house near the visitor centre. Unlike the real houses, which you look down into, you can actually walk inside this one and get a feel for how cosy, dark and smoky life must have been. Kids love it, and it really helps make sense of what you see on the walk.
The coast here is battered by Atlantic storms, and erosion is a real threat to the site, which makes seeing it feel even more special.

Allow around one and a half to two hours. Then explore more of the West Mainland: the cliffs at Yesnaby are spectacular, and the Brough of Birsay is a tidal island with Pictish and Norse remains, though you must check the tide times before crossing. Stromness, with its narrow flagstone street, is a lovely spot for something to eat.
